blocks.p: You might have a general understanding of the Polyvagal Theory and the primary and mixed states. But there's a lot of information out there, and a lot of the Polyvagal Theory influencers mix up terminology, or don't match from person to person. That can leave you confused. It'd be nice to have a better understanding of how these autonomic states show up in the real world.

So first I'll do a quick breakdown of all the official Polyvagal Theory autonomic states, with the correct terminology. Then I'll share the story of Courtney, and we'll apply what we learned to it. You'll be better able to spot the states in the story, and in yourself as well.

For context, I'm on the Polyvagal Institute's editorial board. This stuff is kind of my life. You could say I'm obsessed with it. I spend pretty much zero time taking in other sources of Polyvagal Theory information. I go to the primary source: mostly Dr. Porges, his books and the papers he writes, and Deb Dana as well.

The basic idea is that the body can be prepared for more safety or more defense. To put it super simply, the body has different states in preparation for connection, for responding to danger, or even for responding to life threat.
There are three primary states: safety, flight and fight, and shutdown.

ul: Safety is the state where your body is prepared to connect: with yourself, with the environment, or with somebody else.

Flight and fight is the sympathetic state. Your body is prepared to run away or fight. We can also call it the mobilization state, because you're not always running away or fighting when you're in it. Basically, it's for mobilization.
Shutdown is for immobilization in danger. It's for when there's a life threat, when the body needs to collapse and feign death.

blocks.p: Think of the primary states like primary colors: red, yellow, and blue. Primary colors exist on their own. You can't mix anything to get them. But you can mix primary colors to get secondary colors. In the Polyvagal Theory, when you mix primary states, you get mixed states. They're sometimes called hybrid states. I always call them mixed states.
The three original mixed states, as I think of them, are freeze, play, and stillness.

ul: Freeze is immobilization, just like shutdown, but a different flavor. Freeze is immobilization with tenseness: the muscles are tense, the heartbeat is high. Freeze is like paralysis. It's a combination of shutdown and flight and fight, so the body is mobilized but also immobile at the same time.
Play is a combination of the safe and social state plus flight and fight. Safe and connected, but also mobile.

Stillness is where you're immobile but safe. Immobile, but okay with it. Lying down to go to sleep, meditating, even using the restroom: all of these require that you're immobile, but you're okay with it. You probably have some stillness in your system right now.

blocks.p: Three more mixed states were officially added later, I think in 2023: appease, fawn, and intimacy. Appease and fawn had been discussed before, but they were officially recognized in Our Polyvagal World.

Appease also came out in a paper discussing appeasement in comparison to Stockholm syndrome. Appease is the activation of all of the states: safety plus flight and fight plus shutdown. There's an element of each one in it. To put it super simply, appeasement is the ability to use social cues to lessen the threat during an ongoing, life-threatening scenario. That's my best understanding of it. This would be like a hostage situation. If you think of Stockholm syndrome, think of appeasement.

Fawn is different from appease. Fawn is said to be a combination of flight and fight with shutdown. I personally find this lacking. There's no real deep paper written on it. It's only very briefly mentioned in Our Polyvagal World, and I find the way it's described to be lacking.

I conceptualize fawn as mostly a dissociative shutdown state. The primary state is shutdown, plus, I suppose, flight and fight. But the behaviors of fawn, the complete surrendering of the self, sacrificing one's values, appearing as a non-threat to a captor or an abuser, are different from trying to connect with them, like with appeasement. Fawn says, "I'm going to anticipate your needs, and I am not a threat." I think that requires a huge dissociative shutdown. I'd actually argue appease does as well, but neither is really discussed that way in the Polyvagal Theory literature, as far as I've seen. I don't know how someone does the behaviors of appeasement and fawn without a very significant amount of dissociative shutdown.

Intimacy is said to be shutdown plus safety. But we already know shutdown plus safety equals stillness. The difference is that intimacy involves another variable: a safe other is present. So basically, intimacy is stillness plus a safe other.
I've shared my questions and concerns about the validity and necessity of the newer mixed states in other episodes. For now, that's the brief rundown.

As you read Courtney's story, see if you can identify when these states are active within her, or within the other people in the story, and when they change. Mainly, look for the primary states: safe and social, flight and fight, and shutdown. Play and freeze are probably present too, and maybe a little stillness. I didn't explicitly try to put the newer mixed states in, but you might find their flavor in here as well.

This story comes from my book Trauma and the Polyvagal Paradigm, where it shows up a few times to illustrate what states are active as I talk about them. There's nothing super graphic here, but there is some flavoring of things that might be reminiscent of trauma. I don't know what's triggering for you, so take this as a heads up before you continue.

Courtney is a fictionalized representation of an actual therapy client. Her story illustrates a sequence of going from the safe and social state down the polyvagal ladder. We'll catch up with her after each state to unfold her story.

Courtney is a really sweet, kind-hearted, soft-spoken sixteen-year-old girl. The story begins at her aunt's house. The house acts as a gathering place for lots of family, friends, and neighbors. There's a front house and a smaller back house. Her uncle lives in the back house, where he needs constant tending, because he's unable to walk on his own or do basic self-care. People come and go from the back house to check on him and tend to him.

Courtney and her friends like to hang out in the back house and watch TV or mess around on their phones. On this particular day, that's what they're doing. They're smiling and laughing. They make eye contact, and they play fight with each other. Courtney checks on her uncle and makes sure he's tended to. She's compassionate. She looks her uncle in the eyes gently and smiles at him with eye crinkles.
What state does Courtney have access to so far, and how can you tell?

If you guessed her safety state, I'd agree. She's very well anchored in it. She's able to check on her uncle, and she's connected with her friends. She also has access to a mixed state: play. She and her friends were able to play fight. So she has plenty of safe and social activity within her, but also some mobility. That's play. All of them are well anchored in their safety state right now.
Courtney's aunt's house is a gathering place for many people, and Courtney knows most of them. But on this particular day, a strange man comes to the back house, where she and her friends are.

Courtney and her friends see him come in through the front door. He makes eye contact with them, but his eyes are kind of wide, and he just sort of stares. He doesn't say anything, and he doesn't smile or do anything to indicate that he's friendly. He walks to the back of the house to check on the uncle. Courtney feels a bit of hesitance and discomfort. She goes back to watching TV with her friends, and they don't think or talk about him.

Then the man comes back out after a few minutes. He stands in the room with the TV, where they are, and asks how old they are. They feel uncomfortable, but they say their ages: 16, 17, and 17. One of the girls tells him she has a boyfriend. The other tells him they're too young for him and he doesn't need to worry about it.

The man looks at Courtney and asks if she has a boyfriend. She says no, with an uncomfortable laugh. He asks if she wants to go to the back room with him to check on her uncle, and she says no. Her friends chime in and tell him to leave them alone. They're too young for him, and he's acting weird.

Courtney feels an impulse to leave, but also feels stuck in her spot, terrified of this strange man who is far bigger than her. He approaches the three girls, and his tone gets more firm. "Little girls shouldn't be talking to no man like that," he says. The two friends scoff and ignore him. Courtney stays still, ready to run, but scared into immobilization.

The man storms off down the hallway and out of sight. Courtney thinks she should leave. She tells her friends, and they agree. But first she has some stuff in the back room she needs to collect. She sticks her head around the wall and peers down the hallway, feeling anxious and breathing shallow. The strange man is in the bathroom at the end of the hallway. So she quietly crosses the hall into the room with her stuff, closes the door behind her, and starts getting her things together.
Then she hears his voice outside the room. "Hey, you in there? Let me come in."
Courtney laughs nervously. "Yeah, I'm in here. I'll be out soon," she says.

The man starts to open the door, and Courtney grabs it and pulls it shut. "I said let me in there with you," he says. The two of them are pulling on the door handles. She keeps laughing, trying to play it off as a joke. Her friends get involved and get him to back off. They tell him again he's being weird and start yelling at him to leave her alone.

The man stops with a huff. He yells into the air about little girls respecting grown men. Courtney comes out of the room with her stuff and heads straight to the front door with her friends. Her friends keep yelling as they get to the front door. The man follows, yelling at them not to leave. He grabs Courtney by the arm, pulling her close to him.

Her friends are yelling at him, commanding him to stop, but he's ignoring them completely, 100 percent focused on Courtney. Courtney has stopped trying to laugh things off at this point. She's louder now, yelling at him to let go. She's using one arm to pull his hand off her other arm. She and her friends begin to hit him as they yell directly at him, commanding him to stop. But he's big. Very big, and very dominant.
Courtney and her friends make so much noise that the people from the front house respond and make their way to the back house. One of Courtney's uncles intervenes, and the strange man backs off.
What states do you see in Courtney, or in her friends? When did you notice the shifts happening?

Once the man entered the back house, they probably experienced some flight activation. It seemed like Courtney felt that, but they didn't act on it. He left the room, and they kind of left it at that.

Pretty quickly, they shifted down to fight activation, especially once Courtney was in the room and they were pulling on the door from both sides. Her friends definitely acted on their fight activation. It took Courtney longer, but she did eventually use her fight activation, yelling directly at him and commanding him, enough to get the attention of the other people on the property.

You could also argue there's some freeze activation here. Courtney feels tense and kind of laughs it off. That's activation without acting on it: the flight and fight is activated, but she's not acting on it. She's just kind of frozen, immobile in place. Even at the very beginning, when there wasn't any direct confrontation, she felt that flight activation but also felt immobilized in place. That could be a little freeze.

The strange man laughs it off and marches to the front house, finally leaving the girls alone. Courtney and her friends explain what happened to the aunt and the others who gathered around. They explain how he was acting weird, how he tried to be alone with Courtney, and how he grabbed at her. They tell them everything, using their voices loudly and forcefully. They demand that action be taken, that the uncles, quote unquote, beat his ass.

Her aunt says, "We heard you yelling, then we checked the security cameras and saw everything before coming down here." The aunt looks Courtney up and down and says, "He wouldn't act that way if you didn't lead him on."
Courtney is stunned. Her eyes go wide, and she stands still. "Lead him on?" she checks. "I'm wearing a t-shirt, Auntie. We were just watching TV."
"I've seen you and your friends back here before. I've seen you talking to the men and tying up your shirts and showing your skin."
Courtney feels the energy leave her body. She goes numb, and her shoulders slump.
The aunt continues. "Don't be coming around here no more. You and your little friends can go somewhere else."
Courtney hangs her head and walks slowly off. Her friends put their arms around her, yelling back at the aunt about what really happened, how wrong this is, and how they don't deserve this.
What did you notice here, particularly the difference between freeze and shutdown?
The energy just drains out of Courtney. It leaves her body. She slumps down, her head's down, and she walks off. She seems very defeated. That's shutdown, in a real-life scenario.

She didn't flat-out immobilize, collapse, and faint. That would be the extreme version of shutdown, maybe in a truly life-threatening scenario. But in this scenario, she is not safe. She can't run away from it. She kind of could fight against it, but she still isn't safe. There's no repercussion for the man, no justice. He's still there, and he's still very much a threat. And the people in her life who are supposed to care about her the most and protect her are not doing that. So she goes into shutdown, and the energy leaves her body.

I know, that's super depressing, and kind of a low note to leave on. But when this person came to me in therapy (and of course this is heavily anonymized), we were able to process it, and she was able to climb her polyvagal ladder by talking about the situation and coming out of shutdown. It definitely lingered in her system for quite a while.

But she came out of shutdown and was able to feel empowerment. She actually talked to her aunt about it and put in a really, really healthy boundary. Basically, she was done going there. She carried that momentum and started really advocating for herself, using her fight energy together with her safety state: using her power to put in and enforce healthy boundaries with a number of people in her life. She kind of kicks butt.

I'm sad she had to go through this, but she definitely grew from it, processed it, and empowered herself. Hopefully you can now see some of the polyvagal states in action, and how they could realistically look day to day, in her story and in your own.
